Joint position targets are a common imitation baseline; ACT predicts chunks of absolute joint-and-gripper targets for two ViperX arms <Cite id="act-aloha-2023" />. The controller interpolates and enforces limits, but one shoulder angle moves different arms differently.

Joint velocity targets drift when integrated; the [kinematics module](/classical/kinematics/) derives the forward map and Jacobian both need <Cite id="modern-robotics-2017" />. In locomotion RL, target joint angles with local feedback beat raw torques for learning speed, robustness and motion quality <Cite id="peng-action-space-2016" />.

Cartesian actions say what the tool should do. Once range and frame are fixed, relative deltas from the current pose label arms with different joint counts and link lengths alike, provided each robot supplies inverse kinematics or an operational-space controller; Khatib's 1987 operational space formulation unifies motion and force control <Cite id="khatib-1987" />. X-VLA instead learns a separate set of soft-prompt embeddings for each data source as embodiment-specific prompts <Cite id="x-vla-2025" />.

Torque actions expose dynamics and contact; Levine et al. mapped raw images to motor torques <Cite id="levine-visuomotor-2015" />. Impedance actions sit between: the policy picks a pose target plus stiffness and damping, and a controller turns error into force. <Term id="behavior-cloning">Behavior cloning</Term> is imitation learning cast as supervised learning: a policy $\pi(a \mid s)$ is regressed onto [expert actions](/how-robots-work/#puppeteer) given expert observations. In closed loop the robot's own actions choose its future inputs, breaking the i.i.d. assumption, so <Term id="compounding-error">errors compound</Term> <Cite id="ross-bagnell-2010" />.

## Origins in driving

ALVINN (1988), a three-layer back-propagation network with camera and laser-range inputs, trained on simulated road images and was tested on NAVLAB, a modified Chevy van <Cite id="alvinn-1988" />. Later driving systems added off-centre, rotated training views <Cite id="bojarski-e2e-driving-2016" />, or synthesized perturbations once 30 million examples proved too few <Cite id="chauffeurnet-2018" />.

<Image id="navlab-1-5-cmu-2017" />

## Covariate shift, stated precisely

Training data follow the expert's state distribution $d_{\pi^*}$; the robot visits its own $d_\pi$, drifting further with each mistake <Cite id="dagger-2011" />. Ross and Bagnell (2010) proved a regret bound that grows quadratically in the horizon $T$ <Cite id="ross-bagnell-2010" />. The DAgger paper restates their bound for expert-distribution error $\varepsilon$ bounding the 0-1 loss and task cost in $[0,1]$, and notes it is tight <Cite id="dagger-2011" />:

$$
J(\pi) \leq J(\pi^*) + T^2\varepsilon
$$

With log-loss, behavior cloning reaches horizon-independent sample complexity when payoff range and policy-class complexity are controlled <Cite id="foster-bc-horizon-2024" />, though a tabular lower bound of order $|S|T^2/N$ survives even active expert queries <Cite id="rajaraman-il-limits-2020" />. With continuous actions, smooth deterministic imitators can suffer execution error exponentially larger in the horizon than their training error <Cite id="simchowitz-continuous-il-2025" />.

<Image id="covariate-shift" />

## Training-side problems

On demonstrations with several valid strategies, energy-based implicit policies often beat mean-squared-error and mixture-density policies <Cite id="implicit-bc-2021" />, and <Term id="diffusion-policy">Diffusion Policy</Term> learns both Push-T modes, committing to one per rollout <Cite id="diffusion-policy-2023" />. Pan et al. (2025) attribute generative policies' benchmark gains to iterative computation instead of multimodality <Cite id="much-ado-noising-2025" />.

A single Markovian state cannot predict pauses, so single-step policies freeze, as ACT and Diffusion Policy document <Cite id="act-aloha-2023" /> <Cite id="diffusion-policy-2023" />. Temporal context is the usual fix, yet more input information can worsen a cloned policy under shift <Cite id="causal-confusion-2019" />, and a history-conditioned policy can cheat by copying the expert's previous action <Cite id="copycat-bc-2020" />.

Behavior cloning at best matches its demonstrator, and robomimic found results depend on demonstration quality and checkpoint selection <Cite id="robomimic-2021" />. Past a threshold, extra demonstrations per environment or object barely help; diversity matters far more <Cite id="lin-data-scaling-laws-2024" />. In Park and Levine's OCBench (October 2026), whose scripted demonstrators mimic human ones, success can keep rising as a policy overfits, and on two tasks closed-loop policies almost completely fail where action chunking works <Cite id="ocbench-2026" />.

## DAgger: relabel the states you actually visit

<Term id="dagger">DAgger</Term> (Dataset Aggregation) labels the states the learner visits, reducing <Term id="imitation-learning">imitation learning</Term> to no-regret online learning <Cite id="dagger-2011" />.

<Image id="navlab-1-5-cmu-2017" />

Training data follow the expert's state distribution $d_{\pi^*}$; the robot visits its own $d_\pi$, drifting further with each mistake <Cite id="dagger-2011" />. $$

$$

The design question is how to get actions out of a model that outputs text . ## RT-1: actions become tokens RT-1 (2022) conditions an ImageNet-pretrained EfficientNet on the instruction through FiLM , and TokenLearner cuts each of six images to eight tokens for a 19M-parameter decoder-only transformer; the full system has 35M parameters . Its 11 action coordinates are seven arm variables (translation, rotation and gripper opening), three base variables and a mode switch that can also end the episode. Each is discretized into 256 bins spaced uniformly within its bounds and trained with categorical cross-entropy . Drag “Moment in the movement” to watch each motion's value land in one of 256 bins. The data covers about 130k episodes over more than 700 tasks, collected over 17 months with 13 robots, and the paper reports 3,000 real-world evaluation trials .
RT-1 predicts one action at a time at 3 Hz, with a fixed 280 ms wait, the maximum observed latency of all components, to keep action timing consistent . ## RT-2: actions become text RT-2 (2023) writes each action dimension's 256 bin indices as strings in a vision-language model's token stream: PaLI-X already has a token for every integer up to 1000, while PaLM-E overwrites its 256 least frequently used tokens. Octo ships 27M- and 93M-parameter checkpoints trained on 800k Open X-Embodiment trajectories; learned readout tokens in a block-wise-masked transformer feed a lightweight diffusion head that outputs action chunks, and fine-tuning can add a new sensor or output while retaining the transformer weights . GR00T N1 separates the two, with a vision-language System 2 over a diffusion-transformer System 1 . π0.7 conditions on language plus strategy metadata and subgoal images, and Physical Intelligence reports zero-shot cross-embodiment laundry folding . Google DeepMind's Gemini Robotics 2 controls full humanoids, including a 22-degree-of-freedom hand, and is available only to early-access partners .

PaLM-E's inputs interleave visual, continuous state-estimation and text embeddings, grounding its language model in sensor observations . Trained on 970k robot demonstrations, it predicts seven coordinates for position, orientation and gripper, each split into 256 uniform bins between the training data's 1st and 99th quantiles instead of its minimum and maximum; bin indices replace the 256 least-used Llama tokens and are predicted autoregressively . CogACT conditions a dedicated diffusion action transformer on the VLM's output . ## The discrete-token throughput problem OpenVLA's original formulation decodes seven action tokens sequentially per timestep . RT-2 runs at 1 to 3 Hz for the 55B PaLI-X variant and about 5 Hz for the 5B variant, queried over the network from a multi-TPU cloud service . OpenVLA runs at about 6 Hz on one RTX 4090 in bfloat16, without compilation or speculative decoding, and its quantization analysis notes that slower inference changes the controller dynamics . π0 instead adds a flow-matching expert that outputs action chunks at up to 50 Hz , and PD-VLA decodes in parallel by fixed-point iteration with no retraining, reaching 2.52 times the execution frequency . The demonstrations follow one consistent strategy per task, and the authors leave multimodal demonstrations and large-scale pretraining open . OFT changed both throughput and success without replacing OpenVLA . Write down the required semantic novelty, embodiment data, action contract and latency budget, pick the prior with the [foundation-model guide](/manipulation/foundation-models/) and the output with the [action-space guide](/manipulation/action-spaces/), then compare only models whose contracts match; [generalist policies](/manipulation/generalist-policies/) and [RL fine-tuning](/manipulation/rl-finetuning/) cover the rest. GR00T N1 separates the two, with a vision-language System 2 over a diffusion-transformer System 1 . π0.7 conditions on language plus strategy metadata and subgoal images, and Physical Intelligence reports zero-shot cross-embodiment laundry folding . Google DeepMind's Gemini Robotics 2 controls full humanoids, including a 22-degree-of-freedom hand, and is available only to early-access partners .

ChatVLA calls this spurious forgetting, robot training overwriting visual-text alignments . Later models changed tokenization, training data, memory and prompting. Drag the integration steps slider from 1 upward to watch the cloud reach the action modes. ## π0: the action expert π0 grafts a second transformer, the action expert of about 300M parameters, onto a pretrained vision-language model initialized from PaliGemma; the backbone handles image and text tokens, and the expert's 50 action tokens attend into it at every layer through shared self-attention. Inputs are 2 or 3 RGB images, language and proprioceptive state, and the model predicts H = 50 actions, executing 16 per inference at 20 Hz on UR5e and Franka or 25 at 50 Hz on the other robots . Where [Diffusion Policy](/manipulation/diffusion-policy/) denoises with a DDPM, π0 trains the expert with conditional flow matching on a straight path. Training samples noise $\varepsilon \sim \mathcal{N}(0, I)$, forms $A_t^\tau = \tau A_t + (1 - \tau)\varepsilon$, and regresses $v_\theta$ onto $u = A_t - \varepsilon$. Inference integrates from $\tau = 0$ to $\tau = 1$ in 10 forward-Euler steps, with the image-text-state prefix KV-cached once so each step recomputes only the action suffix . Lipman et al. found optimal-transport paths more efficient than diffusion paths for training and sampling .
Cross-embodiment pre-training combines single-arm, dual-arm and mobile manipulators across 7 robot configurations. The base model reaches what the authors call "rudimentary proficiency", and complex tasks such as laundry folding use curated post-training data . PI says π0, π0-FAST and π0.5 executed chunks synchronously, waiting for inference after each one , which the RTC paper later compared with asynchronous execution on π0.5 . ## Why ten steps is enough A DDPM path curves through noise space, while rectified flow straightens paths so that coarse time steps simulate them accurately . Each Euler step costs a forward pass through the expert: π0 uses 10 steps , π0.6 uses five , and π0.7 also uses five . Consistency and one-step distillation, covered in [Diffusion Policy](/manipulation/diffusion-policy/), pursue the same saving. ## π0-FAST: compressed action tokens FAST traces the failure of per-dimension, per-timestep binning to highly correlated tokens, which make next-token prediction trivial; policies with this naive tokenization make no progress on table bussing at 20 Hz or T-shirt folding at 50 Hz . FAST instead applies a discrete cosine transform along time, rounds the coefficients and byte-pair-encodes the result, and its universal FAST+ tokenizer is trained on about one million one-second action chunks across embodiments , or "1M real robot action sequences" in PI's post . Trained on a 10k-hour cross-embodied mixture, π0-FAST matches π0's generalist performance with up to five times fewer GPU hours. Inference costs more: about 750 ms per one-second chunk on an NVIDIA 4090, against within 100 ms for diffusion π0, since decoding needs 30 to 60 tokens instead of ten steps . It keeps the π0 skeleton, adds training examples that interleave images, language commands, object detections, subtask predictions and low-level actions, and at inference first predicts a language subtask ("pick up the plate"), then conditions the action expert on it. In long-horizon mobile manipulation in new homes, removing either cross-embodiment data source significantly hurts home-task scores, while removing web data leaves those scores nearly unchanged but strongly hurts language following and subtask inference . The Knowledge Insulation paper turns the two-stage π0.5 approach into one stage: the expert trains with flow matching for continuous inference, and the backbone trains on discrete FAST tokens, vision-language data and planning data, with expert gradients stopped at the backbone keys and values . With a frozen backbone, shirt folding drops to 0%; on generalist table bussing, π0 needs 7.5 times as many training steps to match; and vision-language co-training also gives the joint-training baseline good language following without stop-gradient . The report places this formulation closest to CFGRL , while outside groups find RL on flow-based π0 and π0.5 hard because flow matching makes action log-likelihoods intractable . The companion blog's example is a bad portafilter grasp that causes a later insertion failure . On a rig with two 6-DoF arms and 50 Hz joint-position control, on-robot experience more than doubles successful completions per hour for double-shot espresso and diverse laundry, tested on a button-up shirt, against offline RL plus demonstration fine-tuning. Failures fall by "about a factor of two" ("more than 2×" in the figure), the "90%+" summary excludes diverse laundry, and the box task reports stages separately, with remaining failures mostly in final placement . PI published MEM on March 3, 2026 . π0.6-MEM pairs a video encoder with a high-level policy that predicts updated natural-language summaries of earlier events, and handles tasks needing up to fifteen minutes of memory, such as recipe setup and kitchen cleanup. It is π0.6 plus MEM at about 5B parameters, and training simulates real-time chunking delays of 0 to 12 timesteps, up to 240 ms on a 50 Hz robot , the training-time RTC method that on π0.6 matched inference-time RTC at lower compute . The context holds task and subtask language, with the subtask from a learned high-level policy or a human, and episode metadata on quality, speed and mistakes; training uses different subsets of this context but always keeps the joint or end-effector control-mode label. Multi-view subgoal images come from a BAGEL-initialized world model, and subgoal and subtask generation run in separate threads . BAGEL is a unified decoder-only model pretrained on trillions of interleaved tokens . π0.7 folds laundry on a bimanual UR5e with no laundry data for that robot, matching the task progress of experienced teleoperators trying it there for the first time . In the air-fryer example, language coaching fine-tunes a high-level policy that generates the subtasks without new teleoperation, which the authors call "early signs of compositional task generalization" . [Human video](/manipulation/cross-embodiment/) joins the line through π0.5 co-fine-tuning, which roughly doubles performance on scenarios seen only in human data . ## Which checkpoints are listed PI released π0's code and weights in openpi on February 4, 2025, saying 1 to 20 hours of data sufficed to fine-tune a variety of tasks . The openpi README at the pinned commit of August 24, 2026 lists base checkpoints for π0, π0-FAST and π0.5, plus π0-FAST, π0 and π0.5 models fine-tuned on DROID and a π0.5 LIBERO model . DROID holds 76k trajectories from 564 scenes , and LIBERO has 130 tasks in four suites . <Image id="robocat-embodiments-2023" />

## What must be specified

A claim names its pretraining data, objective, interface and adaptation budget. Data spans web text and images, human video, robot trajectories and simulation; Open X-Embodiment pools 22 robots from 21 institutions <Cite id="open-x-embodiment-2023" />. Objectives include next-token prediction, contrastive learning, video prediction and action denoising.

Budgets run from zero-shot prompting through parameter-efficient and full fine-tuning to new robot data at scale. RoboCat adapts to new tasks and robots from 100 to 1,000 examples <Cite id="robocat-2023" />, Octo fine-tunes to new sensors and action spaces in hours on consumer GPUs <Cite id="octo-2024" />, and π*0.6's RL from experience more than doubles throughput on some of the hardest tasks <Cite id="pistar06-2025" />. The newest rung is in-context learning: Generalist reports GEN-1.5 learning a task from one 3 to 12 second demonstration with no training <Cite id="gen-1-5-2026" />.

Robota-Embed, from Yunze Liu, Linxi Fan, Han Cai and colleagues at NVIDIA, MIT, UC Berkeley, Oxford and CMU (October 2026), encodes vision, language and action in one vector, so a robot can retrieve recorded experience as context. Seeding a frozen DreamZero policy with a retrieved video, chosen by a reranking agent, raised its average success on three simulated DROID-Sim tasks from 47.0% to 56.3% over 100 trials per task, while random reference videos lowered it to 36.0%. Without the reranker, its top-1 retrievals reached 50.3% against 43.3% for Omni-Embed-Nemotron-3B <Cite id="robota-embed-2026" />.

## VLA foundations

RT-1 argued for task-agnostic training of high-capacity models on diverse robot data <Cite id="rt1-2022" />. RT-2 co-fine-tunes a vision-language model on robot trajectories and internet-scale vision-language tasks, writing actions as reserved tokens <Cite id="rt2-2023" />, and OpenVLA made a comparable recipe public on Open X-Embodiment <Cite id="openvla-2024" />. VLAs still struggle with novel robot setups until fine-tuned: OpenVLA-OFT's recipe lifted OpenVLA's average success across four task suites from 76.5% to 97.1% <Cite id="openvla-oft-2025" />.

π0 pairs a pretrained VLM with a separate flow-matching expert for continuous action chunks <Cite id="pi0-2024" />. π0.5 credits its generalization to co-training on heterogeneous tasks <Cite id="pi05-2025" />, and π0.7's authors call their 2026 model a steerable generalist robotic foundation model <Cite id="pi07-2026" />.

Test-time training stores past observations in fast weights that gradient descent updates while the policy runs. RoboTTT (July 2026) extends visuomotor context to 8K timesteps without growing inference latency and averaged a 79% task completion score on long-horizon real-robot tasks, against 42% for the single-step-context GR00T N1.7 baseline <Cite id="robottt-2026" />. ECoMEM (Stanford, September 2026) keeps an explicit record of task facts that a learned reader turns into memory tokens for the VLA, reaching 86.1% success on two new real-robot tasks against 8.6% without memory <Cite id="ecomem-2026" />.

IMPRINT, from Yilin Wu, Homanga Bharadhwaj, Guanya Shi and colleagues at Amazon FAR and Carnegie Mellon (October 2026), trains a latent memory of past camera frames, actions and joint states with the policy, so no rule has to pick which frames to keep. On the nine memory-dependent RMBench simulation tasks, with 100 trials per task, it raised π0.5 from 25.4% to 72.8% average success; EventVLA, the strongest of six memory baselines, reports 67.8%. The recurrent version took 122.8 ms per 50-step action chunk on an L40S GPU, against 91.0 ms for π0.5 without memory and 960 ms for EventVLA <Cite id="imprint-2026" />.

## Humanoid foundations

GR00T N1 combines a vision-language module with a diffusion transformer, trained on real-robot trajectories, human videos and synthetic datasets <Cite id="gr00t-n1-2025" />. For a humanoid, morphology, whole-body balance and shared action coordinates set the reuse boundary. Figure pretrained [Helix 2.5](/manipulation/generalist-policies/) from random initialization entirely on Index, its dataset of human behavior; with identical task data, it succeeded on 56% of zero-shot trials in 30 unseen homes, against 9% for a policy trained from scratch <Cite id="helix-2-5-2026" />.

<Image id="gr00t-n1-gr1-tasks-2025" />

## Predictive foundations

V-JEPA 2 learns representations from over 1M hours of internet video, then trains an action-conditioned stage on fewer than 62 hours of unlabeled DROID video <Cite id="vjepa2-2025" />. R3M's embedding, pretrained on Ego4D human video, beats from-scratch training by over 20% <Cite id="r3m-2022" />.

<Image id="cosmos-policy-aloha-2026" />

Cosmos frames a world foundation model as a general-purpose model fine-tuned into custom ones <Cite id="cosmos-predict-2025" />. Cosmos 3 unifies understanding, generation, forward and inverse dynamics and policy outputs in one omnimodal model <Cite id="cosmos-3-2026" />, and Cosmos Policy turns Cosmos-Predict2 into a policy in one post-training stage, reaching 98.5% on LIBERO <Cite id="cosmos-policy-2026" />. Each output needs its own test: Ctrl-World ranks policies without real rollouts <Cite id="ctrl-world-2025" />.

DreamZero (February 2026) is a [world action model](/world-models/taxonomy/) on a pretrained video diffusion backbone that predicts video and actions together; in real-robot tests it more than doubled average task progress on new tasks and environments over state-of-the-art VLAs, and its 14-billion-parameter model ran closed-loop at 7 Hz <Cite id="dreamzero-2026" />.

## What pretraining does not erase

In TRI's blind, randomized trials, multitask pretraining matched from-scratch policies with 3 to 5 times less data <Cite id="tri-lbm-2025" />. VC-1 found no pretrained visual representation universally dominant <Cite id="vc1-2023" />, and Toyota Research Institute's 89-policy study found that robot-only training degrades the backbone's visiolinguistic understanding <Cite id="lbm-cotraining-2026" />. Generalist reports that GEN-1's base model, pretrained on over half a million hours of wearable human data and no robot data, averaged 99% on three tasks with about one hour of robot data per task, against 19% from scratch <Cite id="generalist-gen1-2026" />.

Pretraining leaves calibration and control integration, closed-loop evaluation under perturbation, latency limits and safety cases to the builder. RoboPAIR jailbroke LLM-controlled robots, including a deployed Unitree Go2, often at 100% attack success <Cite id="robopair-2024" />, and a downloadable checkpoint can hide its training mixture, adaptation data or benchmark protocol.

## A comparison framework

<FoundationModelFamiliesTable className="my-6" />

## Evaluating a foundation claim

Look for a matrix: rows vary tasks and environments, columns vary embodiment, adaptation data and evaluation shift. Report the checkpoint, every tuned component, the new robot data and a same-budget from-scratch baseline. VLAs near 95% on LIBERO drop below 30% under modest camera or initial-state perturbations <Cite id="libero-plus-2025" />, and models above 90% fall to 0.0% under LIBERO-PRO's generalized setting <Cite id="libero-pro-2025" />.

<FoundationModelFamiliesTable className="my-6" />

## Evaluating a foundation claim

Look for a matrix: rows vary tasks and environments, columns vary embodiment, adaptation data and evaluation shift. SayCan (2022) scores each skill in a supplied library twice: the LLM rates its description as the next step, and an affordance value estimates whether it can succeed in the current state. On the mobile manipulator, picking uses a multitask language-conditioned behavior-cloning policy, and RL-trained value functions, calibrated before use as probabilities, score skills without a separate model per skill. On a real Franka FR3 and a Rainbow RB-Y1 mobile manipulator the agent received only the task text and the robots' tools.
